title: SQL vs NoSQL at Scale
summary: Where relational databases strain under scale, and what NoSQL trades away to relieve it.

slides.markdown:
A relational database gives you joins, transactions, and a rigid schema by default — and all three get expensive to keep as a system grows. **NoSQL** is not one thing; it's a family of databases that each relax a specific guarantee to buy back scale.

The interview skill isn't "SQL or NoSQL" as a religion — it's naming which guarantee is actually costing you at your numbers, and picking the store that trades away exactly that one.

slides.sectionTitle: Where relational databases start to strain under scale
slides.markdown:
A single Postgres or MySQL instance handles far more than most engineers expect — tens of thousands of QPS on the right hardware. Strain doesn't show up as "too slow" in general; it shows up in specific places: a `JOIN` across billions of rows scans too much, a single writer node caps total write throughput, or the schema needs a `ALTER TABLE` that locks a table too large to touch safely.

The fix isn't always "switch to NoSQL." Read replicas relieve read load, caching relieves repeat reads, and vertical scaling buys time. Reach for NoSQL only once you've named the *specific* constraint replicas and caching can't fix — usually write throughput or data volume beyond one machine.

slides.sectionTitle: What NoSQL actually trades away for scale (joins, transactions, schema)
slides.markdown:
NoSQL databases scale by giving up things that make a single relational node hard to shard. **Joins** mostly disappear — data is denormalized so one query hits one partition instead of stitching rows across nodes. **Multi-row ACID transactions** shrink to single-key or single-partition atomicity, because coordinating a transaction across many nodes is slow and can block under load. **Schema** loosens — documents in the same collection can have different fields, so you can evolve the shape of your data without a blocking migration.

None of these are free wins: denormalization means updating the same fact in several places, and losing multi-row transactions means your application code now owns consistency the database used to guarantee.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: vertical/read-replica scaling vs horizontal partitioning
slides.markdown:
![Relational primary with read replicas scaling only reads, versus a NoSQL store partitioned so each partition takes its own share of reads and writes](assets/replica-vs-partition-scaling.svg)

Read replicas scale reads without touching how writes work — every write still lands on one primary. Horizontal partitioning changes that shape entirely: each partition takes its own slice of both reads and writes, so total write capacity grows as you add partitions.

That's the real axis of the decision: read replicas buy you read capacity cheaply on a relational store; partitioned write capacity is what pushes teams toward NoSQL (or a sharded relational setup — see partitioning-and-sharding).

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: SQL vs NoSQL on consistency, flexibility, query power
slides.markdown:
| | Relational (SQL) | NoSQL |
|---|---|---|
| Consistency | Strong by default, multi-row ACID transactions | Usually per-key/partition; multi-item consistency is your job |
| Schema flexibility | Fixed schema, migrations needed to change it | Flexible — fields can vary per record |
| Query power | Arbitrary joins, ad-hoc queries, aggregations | Fast on the access patterns you designed for; weak elsewhere |
| Write scaling | One primary is the write bottleneck | Partitioned — write capacity grows with nodes |

**How to decide:** if you need ad-hoc queries and strong multi-row consistency, stay relational and scale reads with replicas or caching; if you have one dominant, known access pattern and write volume one node can't absorb, a NoSQL store built for that pattern wins.

**NewSQL** systems (Google Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB) try to keep the relational model — SQL, joins, ACID transactions — while partitioning data across many nodes like a NoSQL store. They do this by replicating a consensus protocol (like Raft or Paxos) per shard and coordinating cross-shard transactions automatically, instead of leaving that coordination to your application.

The trade isn't free: cross-shard transactions cost extra network round trips for consensus, so latency is higher than a single-node relational write. NewSQL is worth knowing as a third option in an interview — it answers "can I keep SQL and still scale writes?" — but it's a newer, more operationally complex piece of infrastructure than either a battle-tested relational database or a mature NoSQL store.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: choosing NoSQL for scale you don't actually have yet
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We might get big someday, so we should build on NoSQL from day one to avoid a migration later."

**Why it's wrong:** NoSQL's scale benefits come paired with real costs today — no ad-hoc joins, application-owned consistency, and query patterns that must be designed up front. Paying that cost before you have the traffic or data volume that needs it just makes early development slower, for a scaling problem you may never hit.

**Correct model:** start relational unless you already know your dominant access pattern and expect write volume or data size one node can't handle soon. It's easier to shard or migrate off a relational database once you can measure the actual bottleneck than to guess at NoSQL's rigid access patterns before you have real traffic.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: when a single primary actually becomes the write bottleneck
slides.markdown:
A well-tuned Postgres primary on solid hardware can commonly sustain somewhere in the range of 5,000-20,000 writes/sec, depending on row size, index count, and durability settings (`fsync` on every commit costs real throughput but is usually non-negotiable for data you can't afford to lose). A service doing 500 writes/sec is nowhere near that ceiling — the "we need NoSQL for scale" conversation is premature there regardless of how large the eventual user base might be.

The ceiling shows up concretely: write latency starts climbing as the primary's disk I/O or WAL flush becomes the bottleneck, usually well before CPU is the constraint, and read replicas don't help at all since they only add read capacity. Once sustained write volume is verifiably approaching that ceiling, and it isn't fixable by batching writes, reducing index count, or upgrading hardware one more tier, that's the point where sharding the relational store or moving to a partitioned NoSQL store becomes a real conversation, not before.

The practical takeaway: this decision should be driven by a measured number against a real ceiling, not a guess about a company's future traffic.

slides.sectionTitle: CAP theorem, concretely: what a NoSQL store actually gives up during a network partition
slides.markdown:
The CAP theorem says that during a network partition (some nodes can't reach others), a distributed store must choose between **consistency** (every read sees the latest write) and **availability** (every request gets a response). Most single-node relational databases sidestep this entirely in normal operation — there's one node, so there's nothing to partition — which is part of why the trade-off feels abstract until you actually distribute the data.

A concrete case: a NoSQL store configured for availability (an **AP** system, like DynamoDB's default eventually-consistent reads) keeps answering reads and writes on both sides of a network split, but a client on the minority side might read stale data until the partition heals and replicas reconcile. A store configured for consistency (a **CP** system, like a Raft-backed store demanding majority acknowledgment) refuses to serve requests on the minority side rather than risk an inconsistent answer, so those requests fail outright until connectivity is restored.

This is the theorem made practical: "my NoSQL store is eventually consistent" isn't a vague caveat, it's a specific, chosen answer to "what happens to reads on the wrong side of a network split," and picking a store means picking which answer your product can tolerate.
